 Early voting concerns were brought to the head of Tennessee elections. Here’s what he said 
 State coordinator of elections Mark Goins says multiple safeguards catch errors before ballots are cast in the tabulator. 
 By Steve Mehling Published : Oct. 21, 2026 at 5:42 PM CDT | Updated : 1 hour ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google What This Story Is About 
 Dozens of Tennessee voters, including Jackie Herrud and Toni Fitzgerald, reported that their selected candidate did not match what registered on ballot marking machines in Davidson and Williamson counties. 
 Why It Matters 
 State coordinator of elections Mark Goins said such mismatches have always traced back to unintended touches rather than vote flipping, and multiple checks and balances exist to catch errors before a ballot is cast. 
 What Happens Next 
 Goins said his office sends both a Republican and a Democratic machine technician to examine equipment whenever an issue is reported, and voters are urged to review the green selection screen, the review page and the paper ballot before submitting. 
 For Context 
 Davidson County used coffee stirrers in 2024 to help voters avoid unintended touches on the screen but later discontinued them after concerns were raised about plastic use. 
 Catch Up 
 Goins said his office had received only one call about the issue before an initial report aired, with a few more calls coming in afterward, including from people who were concerned but had not personally experienced the problem. 
 NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV) - Jackie Herrud and Toni Fitzgerald are among dozens of Tennessee voters who said the candidate they selected on a ballot marking machine did not match what registered on the machine.
 “I kept punching for the Democrat, Jerri Green, and it kept punching back to Marsha Blackburn,” Herrud said.
 “You try to push the button for the candidate that you’re selecting, and it goes to another candidate,” Fitzgerald said.
 State response
 Mark Goins, Tennessee’s coordinator of elections, said his office had received one call about the issue before an initial report aired. Since then, the office has received a few more calls, including one from a person who said they were not reporting a personal incident but were calling because they were concerned after seeing the story.
 Goins said the machines are designed to ensure the intention of the voter is carried through, and there are several checks and balances in the system.
 He said Tennessee counties use different voting equipment, and the process he described applies specifically to the equipment used in Davidson and Williamson counties, where voters have raised concerns.
 “It’s not a vote flipping situation. It’s normally like an unintended touch that they may not even realize,” Goins said.
 He compared it to typing on a phone with long fingernails, saying a fingernail positioned near the top of a selection box could touch a neighboring box without the voter realizing it.
 Asked whether a couple dozen people reporting a similar issue has, in his experience, always been traced to user error, Goins said his office contacts the county and sends both a Republican and a Democratic machine technician to examine the equipment when an issue is reported. 
 “In all the situations, since I’ve been here, that’s exactly what’s occurred. It’s been a scenario where, like an unintended consequence, they may not even know it,” he said.
 Goins said he has never seen a situation where the machines acted on their own. He said machines are tested before each election with Republican and Democratic checks and balances in place, and candidates are invited to send people to watch the testing.
 How the ballot marking process works
 Goins described three points in the voting process where a voter can confirm their selection.
 The first is the voter selection screen. Goins said the best practice is to touch a candidate’s name directly, typically in the center of the box. When touched correctly, the name lights up green, indicating the ballot marking device will mark that selection. 
 If the green light does not appear for the intended candidate, or appears to light up for a different one, Goins said voters should call over a poll official for assistance before casting the ballot.
 The second is a review screen that appears after all selections are made, showing the voter’s choices. If a voter sees an unintended candidate listed, they can back out and reselect, or ask a poll official for help.
 The third is the physical paper ballot produced by the machine. Goins said voters should review the paper ballot before depositing it into the scanner, since that is what the votes are counted on, not the selection screen. He said all scanners display a message asking voters to review their ballot before submitting it.
 “The votes aren’t being counted on the screen... They’re actually being counted on that paper ballot that’s going in the scanner,” Goins said. “For you to vote for a candidate that’s not supposed to be voted for, every one of those checks and balances along the way are going to have to fail.”
 Goins said the ballot marking device does not store any vote. He said the paper record that goes into the tabulator is what is stored and counted.
 Coffee stirrers used in Davidson County in 2024, returning by request
 Goins said Davidson County deployed coffee stirrers in 2024 as a tool voters could request to help avoid unintended touches on the screen. He said Davidson County later moved away from using coffee stirrers after some people raised concerns about the use of plastic.
 Davidson County Administrator of Elections confirmed that coffee stirrers will be available to voters at each early voting location. You do need to request a stirrer when at the polls in order to use it.
 Advice for voters
 Goins said voters should touch a candidate’s name directly, in the center of the box, to ensure the machine registers the correct selection. He said that if voters have issues, they should find a poll official before submitting their ballot.
 Goins also urged voters to review the ballot in advance, including three proposed constitutional amendments that will appear on the ballot. 
 He said the amendments can be read at GoVoteTN.gov and take about eight minutes to read. He said voter turnout during early voting has been close to 100,000 votes a day.
